summary.text: Boole's inequality is a result about the probability of events, stated in a finite version and in a countable version.
The countable version is deduced from the finite one by taking the number of events to infinity and using continuity from below of probability measures.
For a finite number of events it can be generalized to upper and lower bounds on the probability of finite unions, known as the Bonferroni inequalities.

paragraphs.heading: A rule about measures
paragraphs.text: Seen through measure theory, Boole's inequality is one instance of a broader property called the countable subadditivity of measures. That has a useful consequence. The inequality is not limited to probability measures P; it holds for arbitrary measures as well.

paragraphs.heading: Finite and countable versions
paragraphs.text: The inequality comes in a finite version and a countable version. The countable one can be obtained from the finite one. You let the number of events n grow to infinity and then use the continuity from below of probability measures.

paragraphs.heading: Inside one proof
paragraphs.text: One proof takes a point x and names k as the smallest positive integer for which x lies in Aₖ. A later step relies on the fact that when Bᵢ is contained in Aᵢ, P(Bᵢ) is at most P(Aᵢ), and this is true for every i.

paragraphs.heading: The Bonferroni family
paragraphs.text: For a finite number of events, Boole's inequality can be widened into a set of upper and lower limits on how likely a finite union of events is. These are the Bonferroni inequalities, named after Carlo Emilio Bonferroni, with a reference dated 1936. They can be derived from the inclusion–exclusion principle, and Boole's own result is the special case K = 1. Since that principle needs only finite additivity and nonnegativity of P, the Bonferroni inequalities also hold when P is any finite content in the measure-theory sense.

paragraphs.heading: Five estimates at once
paragraphs.text: Here is a practical use. Suppose you estimate five parameters from a random sample and can control each one separately, and you want all five to be good with a 95% chance. One approach is to give each a share of 0.05/5 = 0.01, that is 1%. In other words, each estimate is made good to 99%, for example with a 99% confidence interval, so that the whole set is good with a 95% chance. This is called the Bonferroni Method of simultaneous inference.
